newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Sri Lanka's Vanik to gain from Forbes merger.
newsitem.headline: Sri Lanka's Vanik to gain from Forbes merger.

text.p: The proposed merger between Sri Lanka's Vanik Inc Ltd and Forbes Ceylon Ltd will lead to the formation of a strong merchant bank able to attract big deals, a senior Vanik official said.

Investment bank Vanik said on Thursday it was negotiating to buy Canadian Global Equity Corp's 50 percent stake in Forbes Ceylon. Forbes Ceylon has an issued capital of 240 million 10-rupee (17 cent) shares.

"The short cut to becoming a strong merchant bank with a good balance sheet is to acquire a company with a large asset base, preferably a very liquid one," Justin Meegoda, President and CEO of Vanik told Reuters.

The jewel in the Forbes Ceylon crown is Forbes Capital, which has nearly 1.3 billion rupees in near-cash investments in Canadian and U.S. government securitites with an average annual yield of around five percent, Meegoda said.

The other attraction was that Forbes Capital is the only local firm with a blanket permission from the Exchange Controller to invest abroad, in line with Vanik's strategy of creating a strong presence in South Asian countries.
Meegoda said normally a firm had to seek deal-by-deal permission from the Exchange Controller to invest abroad.
Vanik was also hoping to diversify its income base through the merger and reduce its dependence on capital market operations, Meegoda said.

Through the fully-owned Forbes Ceylon subsidiaries of Forbes Plantation Management, Forbes Services, Forbes Foods, Forbes Real Estate, and Forbes Tourism, Vanik will have access to the lucrative tea sector, warehousing and real estate and the general sales agency for Emirates Airlines.
Vanik is also buying Global Equity Corporation's 100 percent holdings in the three broking firms of Forbes & Walker stock brokers, commodity brokers and tea brokers, Meegoda said.
"To be able to weather storms like 1996, when capital market activities slumped, you need a diversified income flow," he said.

Vanik's net income fell sharply to 25.5 million rupees last year from 100.5 million in 1995 as fee and fund-based income declined along with the economy as a severe drought and power cuts hit agriculture and industry.

"Vanik shareholders are getting access to resources which will help their scrip to gain in value. Shareholders in Forbes Ceylon, where the share price has been about five rupees a 10-rupee share for much of the time, are acquiring future earnings potential," Meegoda said.
Vanik and Forbes Ceylon shares traded at 21 rupees and 7.25 respectively on Wednesday. The stock exchange halted trading in the two shares on Thursday on news of the merger proposal.
Vanik will pay Global Equity nearly 415 million rupees in cash, based on 350 rupees for every 100 Forbes Ceylon shares.
Global Equity will receive four voting and five non-voting Vanik shares for every 100 Forbes Ceylon shares.

It will also get four 10-year Vanik debentures with an annual coupon rate of 15 percent for every 100 Forbes shares. Each debenture includes a warrant, which can be converted to a Vanik share in three years.
"The deal should be good both for Vanik and Forbes shareholders," said Namal Kamalgoda of CTC Eagle Fund Management.
"If Vanik can put the huge pool of resources at Forbes Capital to better use, both groups should benefit," he added.
The merger is expected to go ahead once Vanik gets clearance from the Exchange Controller and the Central Bank. ($1 = 58.8 rupees)
